From a tracked point-uniformizer \(d\) at \(x\) (1011), the point equations of \(1 \cdot x\) are the local-equation system on the pointed cover

\[ \mathcal U(z) = \begin{cases} V & z = x, \\ X \setminus \{ x\} & z \neq x, \end{cases} \]

whose equation on the member at \(x\) is the tracked section \(s\) and whose equation on every other member is the constant \(1\); the germ at \(\eta \) of the equation at \(x\) is the chosen uniformizer.

Proof ▶

The complement \(X \setminus \{ x\} \) is open (503) and contains every \(z \neq x\), so \(\mathcal U\) is a pointed cover. Regularity holds member by member: on \(V\) the germs of \(s\) are nonzerodivisors (1011), and the constant \(1\) is a unit. For overlap ratios, a pair both at \(x\) or both away from \(x\) has equal equations, ratio \(1\); a mixed pair has overlap inside \(V \setminus \{ x\} \), where \(s\) is a unit (1011), so the ratio of \(s\) and \(1\) is a unit. Thus the data is a local-equation system (983), and the germ at \(\eta \) of the equation at \(x\) is \(\mathrm{germ}_\eta (s) = t\).

7.64 The Čech Picard class of a Weil divisor

Assembling the realization of divisors, the class law, and extraction yields the total class map \(D \mapsto \mathcal{O}_{X}(D)\) from Weil divisors to Čech Picard classes, and its kernel: the class map descends to an isomorphism of \(\operatorname{Div}(X)\) modulo principal divisors onto \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)\).

Theorem 1014 Realization of Weil divisors

Every Weil divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) on the curve is the divisor of a meromorphic presentation.

Proof ▶

First realize the one-point divisors \(n \cdot x\). For \(n \ge 0\), induct on \(n\): the divisor \(0 \cdot x = 0\) is realized by the unit presentation (\(\mathrm{presentationDivisor}(1) = 0\), 1007), and \((n+1) \cdot x = n \cdot x + 1 \cdot x\) by the product of a realization of \(n \cdot x\) with the point presentation at \(x\), using additivity (1007), the point-divisor anchor (1013, 1011), and the one-point arithmetic (567). Negative multiplicities use the inverse presentation, whose divisor is negated (1007). A general \(D\) is a finite sum of one-point divisors (566), realized by the product of their presentations, again by additivity.

The Čech Picard class \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(D) = \mathrm{picClass}(D) \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) of a Weil divisor \(D\) is the class of any meromorphic presentation whose divisor is \(D\). It is well-defined, satisfies \(\mathrm{picClass}(\mathrm{presentationDivisor}(P)) = \mathrm{picClass}(P)\) for every presentation \(P\), and the map \(D \mapsto \mathcal{O}_{X}(D)\) is surjective onto \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)\).

Proof ▶

A realizing presentation exists (1014). If \(P, P'\) both have divisor \(D\), the class law (1009) gives \(\mathrm{picClass}(P) = \mathrm{picClass}(P')\), so \(\mathrm{picClass}(D)\) is well-defined; taking \(D = \mathrm{presentationDivisor}(P)\) with the realization \(P\) itself gives \(\mathrm{picClass}(\mathrm{presentationDivisor}(P)) = \mathrm{picClass}(P)\). For surjectivity, every class \(L\) is presented by some \(P\) (999), and then \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(\mathrm{presentationDivisor}(P)) = \mathrm{picClass}(P) = L\).

\[ \mathcal{O}_{X}(0) = 1, \quad \mathcal{O}_{X}(D + D') = \mathcal{O}_{X}(D) \cdot \mathcal{O}_{X}(D'), \quad \mathcal{O}_{X}(\mathrm{div}\, g) = 1 \ (g \in K(X)^{\times }). \]

If \(P, P'\) realize \(D, D'\), then \(P \cdot P'\) realizes \(D + D'\) (1007), so \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(D + D') = \mathrm{picClass}(P \cdot P') = \mathrm{picClass}(P) \cdot \mathrm{picClass}(P') = \mathcal{O}_{X}(D) \cdot \mathcal{O}_{X}(D')\) (1006). Finally \(\mathrm{div}\, g = \mathrm{presentationDivisor}(\mathrm{principal}\, g)\) (1007), so \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(\mathrm{div}\, g) = \mathrm{picClass}(\mathrm{principal}\, g) = 1\) (1006).

7.65 The point-divisor class map and the meromorphic class map coincide

The chapter carries two constructions of the divisor-to-class assignment \(D \mapsto \mathcal{O}_{X}(D)\). The first, \(\mathrm{divisorClass}\) (993), is the finitely supported product of the point-divisor classes \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(x) = \mathrm{picClass}(1 \cdot x)\) read off the point local equations (992); the second, the anchored \(\mathrm{picClass}\) (1015), is the class of any meromorphic presentation realizing \(D\). This closing section identifies them. The bridge is that the point local equations, whose equation at \(x\) has generic-point germ the uniformizer (992), present the one-point divisor \(1 \cdot x\); their two classes agree, and the agreement propagates from one-point divisors to all divisors by homomorphism extensionality.

\[ \mathrm{picClass}(1 \cdot x) \; =\; \mathcal{O}_{X}(1 \cdot x). \]

The presentation of the point-divisor equations has divisor \(1 \cdot x\) (1019), so the anchored class \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(1 \cdot x)\) is the class of that presentation (1015); and the class of the presentation of a local-equation system is the Picard class of the system itself (1000), which is \(\mathrm{picClass}(1 \cdot x)\) (992). Chaining the two equalities gives \(\mathrm{picClass}(1 \cdot x) = \mathcal{O}_{X}(1 \cdot x)\).

The point-product class map (993) and the anchored meromorphic class map (1015) agree on every Weil divisor:

\[ \mathrm{divisorClass}(D) \; =\; \mathcal{O}_{X}(D), \qquad D \in \operatorname{Div}(X). \]
Proof ▶

Both assignments are homomorphisms \(\operatorname{Div}(X) \to \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) from the additive group of divisors to the multiplicative Picard group: \(\mathrm{divisorClass}\) by additivity (994) and the anchored class map by Theorem 1016. Since \(\operatorname{Div}(X)\) is freely generated by the one-point divisors (566), it suffices to check agreement on each \(n \cdot x\). On the point-product side the defining product (993) collapses to the single factor \(\mathrm{divisorClass}(n \cdot x) = \mathrm{picClass}(1 \cdot x)^{n}\). On the anchored side, additivity (1016) gives \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(n \cdot x) = \mathcal{O}_{X}(1 \cdot x)^{n}\). The two base classes are equal, \(\mathrm{picClass}(1 \cdot x) = \mathcal{O}_{X}(1 \cdot x)\) (1020), so their \(n\)-th powers agree and \(\mathrm{divisorClass}(n \cdot x) = \mathcal{O}_{X}(n \cdot x)\). By homomorphism extensionality on the generators, the two maps coincide on all of \(\operatorname{Div}(X)\).

7.66 The unit of the étale sheafification

The honest relative Picard functor maps into its étale-sheafified Layer-2 vehicle \(\mathrm{picEt}\) by a natural transformation — the unit of the sheafification. On an affine test it is the unit of the plus construction; on a general test it is assembled over the affine opens.

For a test object \(T\) and an affine open \(U \subseteq T_{\mathrm{left}}\), the spectrum of the section ring \(\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma (T, U)\) is a test object over \(T\), via the canonical morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma (T,U) \to T\) of the affine open. This assignment is coherent:

  1. (restriction) for \(U \le V\), the map of \(U\) factors through that of \(V\) along \(\operatorname{Spec}\) of the section restriction \(\Gamma (T,V) \to \Gamma (T,U)\);

  2. (naturality) for a morphism of tests \(f \colon T' \to T\) and affine opens \(W \le f^{-1}V\), the square formed by \(\operatorname{Spec}\) of the section pullback \(\Gamma (T,V) \to \Gamma (T',W)\) and the two affine-open test maps commutes;

  3. (top of an affine test) for \(T = \operatorname{Spec}A\), the affine-open test object of the top open, composed with \(\operatorname{Spec}\) of the identification \(\Gamma (\operatorname{Spec}A, \top ) \cong A\) (Definition 911), is the identity of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\).

Proof ▶

The structure morphism to \(\operatorname{Spec}k\) is \(\operatorname{Spec}\) of the \(k\)-algebra structure of the section ring, so the canonical morphism of the affine open lies over \(\operatorname{Spec}k\); this is the compatibility of the affine-open inclusion with the structure morphisms. Coherences (i) and (ii) are both instances of the standard identity \(\operatorname{Spec}(f^{\sharp }_{V,W}) \circ \iota _W = \iota _V \circ f\) for the canonical maps of affine opens, applied to the identity of \(T\) and to \(f\) respectively; (iii) is the fact that the canonical map of the top affine open of an affine scheme is the isomorphism \(\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma (\operatorname{Spec}A, \top ) \cong \operatorname{Spec}A\), inverse to \(\operatorname{Spec}\) of the section identification.

7.67 The degree of a plus class

This section descends it to the plus construction: a plus class over \(K\) is represented on an étale cover, every cover is refined by a single finite separable field extension (cofinality, Theorem 708), and the zigzag shows the field reading is independent of every choice.

Let \(K\) be a field extension of \(k\), \(E\) a presented étale cover of \(K\), and \(x \in \mathrm{relPic}(C, B_E)\) a descent class on \(E\). Let \(L_1, L_2\) be finite separable field extensions of \(K\) and \(j_1 \colon B_E \to L_1\), \(j_2 \colon B_E \to L_2\) two \(K\)-algebra maps. Then

\[ \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{L_1}\bigl(j_1^{*} x\bigr) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{L_2}\bigl(j_2^{*} x\bigr). \]
Proof ▶

Refine the product of the two field covers \(\mathrm{ofField}(L_1) \times \mathrm{ofField}(L_2)\) (Definitions 709, 694) to a single finite separable field extension \(M\) of \(K\) (cofinality, Theorem 708); composing with the coprojections (Definition 695) yields \(K\)-algebra maps \(\theta _1 \colon L_1 \to M\) and \(\theta _2 \colon L_2 \to M\). Then

\[ \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{L_1}(j_1^{*} x) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{M}(\theta _1^{*} j_1^{*} x) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{M}\bigl((\theta _1 j_1)^{*} x\bigr), \]

using invariance of the relative degree under base-field transitions (E-iv-alg descended, Theorem 620) and functoriality (Lemma 713); likewise for the second leg. Now \(\theta _1 j_1\) and \(\theta _2 j_2\) are two \(K\)-algebra maps \(B_E \to M\) out of the cover carrier, and \(x\) is a descent class, so the transport-independence keystone of the plus construction (Theorem 724) gives \((\theta _1 j_1)^{*} x = (\theta _2 j_2)^{*} x\). The two degrees over \(M\) therefore agree, hence so do the original readings.

Theorem 1030 The zigzag: well-definedness of the plus-class degree

Lean declarations

Let \(E_1, E_2, G\) be presented étale covers of \(K\), \(x_1, x_2\) descent classes on \(E_1, E_2\), and \(f \colon B_{E_1} \to B_G\), \(g \colon B_{E_2} \to B_G\) \(K\)-algebra maps with \(f_{*} x_1 = g_{*} x_2\) as descent classes on \(G\) (the identification of the plus-construction setoid). Then for any two field readings — finite separable field extensions \(L_1, L_2\) of \(K\) with \(K\)-algebra maps \(j_1 \colon B_{E_1} \to L_1\) and \(j_2 \colon B_{E_2} \to L_2\) —

\[ \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{L_1}\bigl(j_1^{*} x_1\bigr) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{L_2}\bigl(j_2^{*} x_2\bigr). \]

No Galois theory appears: Galois twisting of the transport is a special case of the transport-independence keystone.

Proof ▶

Refine \(G\) to a single finite separable field extension \(N\) of \(K\) by cofinality (Theorem 708), with refinement map \(\ell \colon B_G \to N\). By leg (i) of the zigzag (Theorem 1029) applied to the descent class \(x_1\) on \(E_1\) and the two readings \(j_1\) and \(\ell f\),

\[ \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{L_1}(j_1^{*} x_1) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{N}\bigl((\ell f)^{*} x_1\bigr) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{N}\bigl(\ell ^{*} f^{*} x_1\bigr) \]

(functoriality, Lemma 713). Cross over along the identification \(f^{*} x_1 = g^{*} x_2\) (the underlying relative classes of \(f_{*}x_1 = g_{*}x_2\), Definition 721) and run the same two steps backwards on the second leg: \(\mathrm{relPicDeg}_{N}(\ell ^{*} g^{*} x_2) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{N}((\ell g)^{*} x_2) = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_{L_2}(j_2^{*} x_2)\), again by leg (i).

The degree \(\deg ^{+}_K \colon \mathrm{PicEtAff}(C, K) \to \mathbb {Z}\) of an étale-locally trivial relative Picard class: represent the class by a descent class \(x\) on a cover \(E\), refine \(E\) to a finite separable field extension \(L/K\) by cofinality (Theorem 708), and read \(\mathrm{relPicDeg}_L\) of the transported class. The value is independent of the representative and of the refinement, and it is pinned by the master equality: for every descent-class representative \((E, x)\), every finite separable field extension \(L/K\) and every \(K\)-algebra map \(j \colon B_E \to L\),

\[ \deg ^{+}_K [E, x] = \mathrm{relPicDeg}_L\bigl(j^{*} x\bigr). \]

In particular, on a field-cover representative \((\mathrm{ofField}(L), y)\) the degree is \(\mathrm{relPicDeg}_L\) of \(y\) transported through the carrier identification.

Proof ▶

Existence of a field refinement of each cover is cofinality (Theorem 708). Independence of the representative is exactly the zigzag (Theorem 1030): two representatives of one plus class are identified after transport to a common refinement (Definition 728), and the zigzag equates any two field readings of such a pair — in particular the readings through the chosen refinements. The master equality is leg (i) of the zigzag (Theorem 1029), comparing the chosen refinement map with the given \(j\); the field-cover normalization is the master equality at the carrier identification of \(\mathrm{ofField}(L)\) (Definition 709).

\(\deg ^{+}_K\) is a homomorphism: \(\deg ^{+}_K(1) = 0\), \(\deg ^{+}_K(a b) = \deg ^{+}_K(a) + \deg ^{+}_K(b)\) and \(\deg ^{+}_K(a^{-1}) = -\deg ^{+}_K(a)\).

Additivity. Represent \(a = [E,x]\) and \(b = [F,y]\) (Lemma 729); the product is represented on the product cover \(E \times F\) by the product of the transported classes (Theorem 733). Inverses. From \(\deg ^{+}(a^{-1}) + \deg ^{+}(a) = \deg ^{+}(1) = 0\).

7.70 Degree-zero preservation under the curve transport

Throughout this section \(k\) is a field, \(D\) and \(E\) (and, where a composite appears, \(F\)) are curve bundles over \(k\) — objects of \(\mathrm{Over}(\operatorname{Spec}k)\), proper, smooth of relative dimension one and geometrically irreducible over \(k\) — and \(g \colon D \to E\) is an arbitrary morphism of \(\mathrm{Over}(\operatorname{Spec}k)\). Pullback along \(g\) preserves degree zero. The degree control is obtained over each field independently: over a field extension \(L\) of \(k\) the base-changed morphism is finite surjective or constant, and in either case a degree-zero class pulls back to a degree-zero class — the multiplier of the finite case is never compared across different fields.

Let \(L\) be a field extension of \(k\) and let \(\Lambda \) be a Čech Picard class on the fibre \((E \otimes \operatorname{Spec}L)_{\mathrm{left}}\) with \(\deg _{\operatorname{Pic}}(\Lambda ) = 0\). Then the pullback of \(\Lambda \) along the whisker \((g \rhd \operatorname{Spec}L) \colon (D \otimes \operatorname{Spec}L)_{\mathrm{left}} \to (E \otimes \operatorname{Spec}L)_{\mathrm{left}}\) satisfies \(\deg _{\operatorname{Pic}}\bigl((g \rhd \operatorname{Spec}L)^{*}\Lambda \bigr) = 0\).

Both fibres \(D_L := (D \otimes \operatorname{Spec}L)_{\mathrm{left}}\) and \(E_L\) are proper, smooth of relative dimension one and geometrically irreducible over \(L\) via their second projections (Theorem 608), and the whisker commutes with the second projections, so it is a morphism of curve bundles over \(L\). By the dichotomy (Theorem 95) it is either finite and surjective, or constant with a single closed point as set-range. In the finite surjective case the generic points match (Lemma 406) and degree multiplicativity (Theorem 635) gives \(\deg _{\operatorname{Pic}}\bigl((g \rhd \operatorname{Spec}L)^{*}\Lambda \bigr) = \bigl[L(D_L) : L(E_L)\bigr] \cdot \deg _{\operatorname{Pic}}(\Lambda ) = 0\). In the constant case the whisker is proper (Theorem 91), in particular quasi-compact, so the pulled-back class is already trivial (Corollary 688), of degree zero.

7.72 Field points across a base-field extension

Let \(k \to L\) be a field extension, \(\sigma : \operatorname{Spec}L \to \operatorname{Spec}k\) the induced morphism, and \(T\) a test object of \(\mathrm{Over}(\operatorname{Spec}L)\). Write \(\sigma _{!}T\) for \(T\) regarded as a test object of \(\mathrm{Over}(\operatorname{Spec}k)\) through \(\sigma \): the same underlying scheme, with structure morphism the structure morphism of \(T\) followed by \(\sigma \); and write \(\operatorname{Spec}K/\operatorname{Spec}F\) for the affine test of an \(F\)-algebra \(K\), as in Chapter 5. This section matches the \(k\)-field-points of \(\sigma _{!}T\) with the \(L\)-field-points of \(T\): a \(k\)-morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}K/\operatorname{Spec}k \to \sigma _{!}T\) from the affine test of a field \(K\) is the same thing as an \(L\)-algebra structure on \(K\) completing the tower \(k \to L \to K\) together with an \(L\)-morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}K/\operatorname{Spec}L \to T\), both directions preserving the underlying morphism of schemes. The matching then exchanges the quantifier defining the degree-zero subgroup on \(\sigma _{!}T\) for a quantifier over \(L\)-field-points of \(T\). For the last two statements, \(C\) is a curve bundle over \(k\) — proper, smooth of relative dimension one, geometrically irreducible — with base change \(C_L := \sigma ^{*}C\) over \(L\) (12).

The composite of the underlying morphism of \(t\) with the structure morphism of \(T\) is a morphism of schemes \(\operatorname{Spec}K \to \operatorname{Spec}L\), hence \(\operatorname{Spec}\) of a unique ring homomorphism \(L \to K\), by full faithfulness of \(\operatorname{Spec}\). These form a scalar tower: the \(k\)-structure map is the composite of \(k \to L\) with the \(L\)-structure map.

Proof ▶

The structure morphism of \(\sigma _{!}T\) is the composite of that of \(T\) with \(\sigma \), so its action on sections over \(U\) factors as \(\Gamma (\operatorname{Spec}k, \top ) \to \Gamma (\operatorname{Spec}L, \top ) \to \Gamma (T, U)\). Under the canonical identifications \(\Gamma (\operatorname{Spec}k, \top ) \cong k\) and \(\Gamma (\operatorname{Spec}L, \top ) \cong L\), the first map is the embedding \(k \to L\) and the second is the \(L\)-structure map of \(\Gamma (T, U)\).

\[ \deg _K\bigl(\mathrm{Sh}_K(x)\bigr) \; =\; \deg _K(x), \]

By the master equality of the plus-class degree (Definition 1031) both sides are read at \((M, j)\): the left side is \(\mathrm{relPicDeg}_M\) of the transport along \(j\) over \(L\) of the shuffled class, which by the naturality square of the relative Picard shuffle (Theorem 717) is the shuffle at \(M\) of the transport along \(j\) over \(k\) of \(y\); by the degree invariance of the relative Picard shuffle at the field \(M\) (Theorem 629) this reads the same integer as the transport itself, which is the right side.

\[ \deg _t(\theta _T) = \deg _{\operatorname{Pic}}(L_0) =: d_1, \qquad \deg _t\bigl(\theta _T^{\, m}\bigr) = m \, d_1 , \]

For a general test \(T\) and field point \(t\), naturality of the family (Definition 1071) plus functoriality of the degree (Theorem 1036) reduce \(\deg _t(\theta _T)\) to the degree of \(\theta _{\operatorname{Spec}K}\) at the identity point of \(\operatorname{Spec}K\), covered by the affine case. For every \(m \in \mathbb {N}\), multiplication by \(\theta _T^{m}\) is a bijection

\[ \mathrm{pic}^0(C,T) \; \xrightarrow {\ \sim \ }\; \mathrm{pic}^{m d_1}(C,T), \qquad \lambda \mapsto \lambda \cdot \theta _T^{m}, \]

natural in \(T\): an isomorphism of set-valued functors from (the underlying-set functor of) \(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{C/k}\) onto the degree-\(m d_1\) layer functor. Backward, \(\mu \mapsto \mu \cdot (\theta _T^{m})^{-1}\) lands in degree zero by additivity (Lemma 1035); the two maps are mutually inverse since the ambient group is commutative. Naturality is naturality of the \(\theta \)-family (Definition 1071): restriction is a homomorphism carrying \(\theta _T^{m}\) to \(\theta _{T'}^{m}\). Transport of a representation along a natural isomorphism of set-valued functors is formal.

Lean declarations

Let \(T\) be a test object and \((O_i)_{i \in \iota }\) an open cover of \(T_{\mathrm{left}}\). Compatible local data on the cover is a family assigning to every index \(i\) and every affine open \(W \le O_i\) a plus class \(v_{i,W} \in \mathrm{PicEtAff}(C, \Gamma (T,W))\), such that (res) within a member, \(v_{i,W}\) restricts to \(v_{i,W'}\) for \(W' \le W \le O_i\), and (glue) across members, \(v_{i,W} = v_{j,W}\) whenever \(W \le O_i\) and \(W \le O_j\). A plus class \(z\) at an affine open \(W\) is a glue value of the data when its restriction to every affine sub-open \(W_0 \le W\) contained in some member \(O_i\) equals \(v_{i,W_0}\).

Compatible local data on an open cover of \(T_{\mathrm{left}}\) has a glue value at every affine open of \(T_{\mathrm{left}}\).

Proof ▶

Fix an affine open \(W\) and choose a finite basic-open refinement \((D(r))_{r \in s}\) of \(W\) subordinate to the cover, with \(\sum _{r \in s}(r) = (1)\) (Theorem 914). The local data restricted to the \(D(r)\) is a compatible family in the sense of the affine Zariski gluing: on an overlap \(D(rr') = D(r) \cap D(r')\) the two restrictions agree by (res) within each chosen member followed by (glue) across the two members. By the affine gluing theorem (Theorem 909) there is a plus class \(z\) at \(W\) restricting to the data on each \(D(r)\).

\(z\) is a glue value: given an affine sub-open \(W_0 \le W\) with \(W_0 \le O_i\), refine \(W_0\) by basic opens of \(W_0\) each of the form \(D(q) \subseteq D(r)\) for some \(r \in s\) (Theorem 914 again). On each such \(D(q)\), the restriction of \(z\) computes through \(D(r)\) as the local datum at \(D(q)\) by (res), and the local datum at \(D(q)\) read through member \(i\) agrees with that read through the member of \(r\) by (glue). So the restrictions of \(z\) and of \(v_{i,W_0}\) to a spanning family of basic opens of \(W_0\) agree, and Theorem 915 concludes.

Let \((f_i \colon T_i \to T)\) have open-immersion left legs and let \(x_i \in \mathrm{picEt}(C, T_i)\) be a family of sections, compatible in the morphism form: for every pair \(i, j\), every test \(Z\) and every pair of morphisms \(g_i \colon Z \to T_i\), \(g_j \colon Z \to T_j\) with \(f_i g_i = f_j g_j\), the two restrictions of the family to \(Z\) agree. The cover value of the family at an affine open \(W\) contained in the range of \(f_i\) is the value of \(x_i\) at the preimage affine open \(f_i^{-1}W\), transported back along the section-ring isomorphism (Lemma 1082). The cover values are compatible local data (Definition 1076) on the ranges \(O_i := \mathrm{range}(f_i)\).

Proof ▶

(res) Restriction within a member commutes with the section-ring transports and with the internal compatibility of the section \(x_i\), by the restriction calculus of the vehicle (Theorem 917) and injectivity of transport along the bijective pullback (Lemma 1082).

(glue) Fix a shared affine open \(W \le O_i \cap O_j\) and form the mediating test: the open subscheme of \(T\) at \(W\), over \(\operatorname{Spec}k\) through the inclusion. The inclusion lifts through both members (an open immersion whose range contains \(W\) admits a lift of the inclusion of \(W\)), producing \(g_i, g_j\) with \(f_i g_i = f_j g_j = (\text{inclusion of } W)\). The compatibility hypothesis identifies the two restricted sections on the mediating test; evaluating both at its top affine open and cancelling the common (bijective) evaluation map (Lemma 1082) identifies the two cover values.

Let \((f_i \colon T_i \to T)\) have open-immersion left legs with jointly surjective ranges. Then two sections of \(\mathrm{picEt}(C,T)\) agreeing after restriction to every member agree; and every compatible family \((x_i)\) as in Definition 1083 glues to a unique section \(s\) with \(f_i^{*} s = x_i\) for all \(i\).

Proof ▶

Separation. At an affine open subordinate to a member the values of the two sections compute through the member’s restriction, which agree; conclude by topological separation (Theorem 924) after cancelling the bijective transports (Lemma 1082).

Gluing. The cover values of the family are compatible local data on the ranges (Definition 1083), which glue to a unique section \(s\) (Theorem 1079). That \(f_i^{*} s = x_i\) is checked at every affine open \(U'\) of \(T_i\): the value of \(f_i^{*}s\) there computes from the value of \(s\) at the image affine open \(f_i(U')\), which is the cover value, i.e. the value of \(x_i\) at \(f_i^{-1}f_i(U') \supseteq U'\), and the internal compatibility of \(x_i\) restricts it to \(U'\). Uniqueness follows from separation.

7.77 The \(\Sigma \)-extension and the big-site sheaf

A presheaf on the slice \(\mathrm{Over}(S)\) extends to a presheaf on the ambient category by summing over structure morphisms. For \(S = \operatorname{Spec}k\) and the degree-zero Picard functor this slice trick produces the big-site carrier consumed by the local-representability engine, and a representation of the extension descends to one of the original functor.

Definition 1086 The canonical slice morphism of an equality

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a category, \(S\) an object, and \(a = b\) two equal morphisms \(T \to S\). The identity of \(T\) is a morphism of slice objects \((T, a) \to (T, b)\) in \(\mathrm{Over}(S)\), the canonical morphism of the equality. It satisfies: the canonical morphism of a reflexive equality is the identity; canonical morphisms compose to the canonical morphism of the transitive equality; and every slice morphism \(g \colon X \to (T, b)\) factors as the canonical morphism of its own compatibility equation followed by the slice morphism induced by its underlying map.

Proof ▶

The identity of \(T\) satisfies \(\operatorname{id}_T \circ b = a\) precisely because \(a = b\); the three laws are immediate from composition of identities.

For a presheaf \(F\) on the slice \(\mathrm{Over}(S)\), the \(\Sigma \)-extension \(\widetilde F\) is the presheaf on the ambient category with

\[ \widetilde F(T) \; :=\; \coprod _{a \colon T \to S} F(T, a) , \]

an element being a pair \(\langle a, \xi \rangle \) of a structure morphism and a fibre element. Restriction along \(g \colon T' \to T\) composes on the structure component and applies \(F\) of the induced slice morphism on the fibre: \(g^{*}\langle a, \xi \rangle = \langle g \circ a,\ F(g)^{*}\xi \rangle \). Two \(\Sigma \)-elements over equal structure morphisms are equal iff their fibres correspond under \(F\) of the canonical morphism of the equality (Definition 1086).

Proof ▶

Functoriality: restriction along the identity composes with \(a\) to \(a\), and the induced slice morphism is the identity, so \(F\) fixes the fibre. For a composite, the two structure components agree by associativity, and the two fibre components correspond under \(F\) of the canonical morphism, since the induced slice morphisms compose accordingly — the transport calculus of Definition 1086 mediates without any cast. The final characterisation of equality of \(\Sigma \)-elements is the elimination rule of the coproduct.

Lemma 1088 The amalgamation seam and the compatibility descent

Let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(\mathrm{Over}(S)\) and \(\widetilde F\) its \(\Sigma \)-extension.

  1. (Amalgamation seam) For \(g \colon T' \to T\), \(a \colon T \to S\), \(b \colon T' \to S\) with \(g \circ a = b\), and elements \(s \in F(T,a)\), \(y \in F(T',b)\): \(g^{*}\langle a, s\rangle = \langle b, y\rangle \) in \(\widetilde F(T')\) iff \(s\) restricts to \(y\) along the slice morphism \((T',b) \to (T,a)\) induced by \(g\).

  2. (Left-leg rule) For a slice morphism \(g \colon Z \to (T,a)\) and \(x \in F(T,a)\): restriction of \(\langle a, x\rangle \) along the underlying map of \(g\) is \(\langle Z_{\mathrm{struct}},\, F(g)^{*}x \rangle \), the honest slice restriction on the fibre.

  3. (Compatibility descent) If two \(\Sigma \)-elements \(\langle a, x\rangle , \langle b, y\rangle \) have equal restrictions along the underlying maps of a pair of slice morphisms \(g_a \colon Z \to (T,a)\), \(g_b \colon Z' = Z \to (T',b)\), then \(F(g_a)^{*}x = F(g_b)^{*}y\).

Proof ▶

(i) After substituting the equality \(g \circ a = b\), both sides live over the same structure morphism and the characterisation of equal \(\Sigma \)-elements (Definition 1087) reduces the claim to the fibres, where the canonical morphism of the reflexive equality acts as the identity. (ii) is (i) applied to the compatibility equation of \(g\), using that the induced slice morphism of the left leg is \(g\) (Definition 1086, factorisation law). (iii) Combine (ii) on both sides: both restrictions are \(\Sigma \)-elements over the structure morphism of \(Z\), and equality of \(\Sigma \)-elements over one structure morphism gives equality of fibres.

Theorem 1089 The \(\Sigma \)-descent of a representation

Uses

Lean declarations

Let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(\mathrm{Over}(S)\) and suppose the \(\Sigma \)-extension \(\widetilde F\) is representable by an object \(J\) of the ambient category, with universal element \(\langle u_1, u_2 \rangle \in \widetilde F(J)\) (the image of \(\operatorname{id}_J\)). Then \(F\) is representable on the slice by \((J, u_1)\), with universal correspondence sending a slice morphism \(g \colon X \to (J,u_1)\) to the slice restriction \(F(g)^{*} u_2\).

Proof ▶

Injectivity. If \(F(g)^{*}u_2 = F(g')^{*}u_2\) then, by the left-leg rule (Lemma 1088(ii)), the restrictions of the universal element along the underlying maps of \(g\) and \(g'\) are the same \(\Sigma \)-element of \(\widetilde F(X_{\mathrm{left}})\); by representability of \(\widetilde F\) the underlying maps agree, hence \(g = g'\) (slice morphisms are determined by their underlying maps).

Surjectivity. Given \(\xi \in F(X)\), the \(\Sigma \)-element \(\langle X_{\mathrm{struct}}, \xi \rangle \) corresponds under the representation to a map \(h \colon X_{\mathrm{left}} \to J\) with \(h^{*}\langle u_1, u_2\rangle = \langle X_{\mathrm{struct}}, \xi \rangle \). Comparing structure components, \(h \circ u_1 = X_{\mathrm{struct}}\), so \(h\) underlies a slice morphism \(g \colon X \to (J, u_1)\); comparing fibres through the amalgamation seam (Lemma 1088(i)) gives \(F(g)^{*}u_2 = \xi \).

Compatibility with composition is functoriality of \(F\).

Theorem 1091 The big-site Zariski sheaf certificate
✓
#

Uses

  • Definition 1090
  • Theorem 1085
  • Lemma 1088

Lean declarations

  • AlgebraicGeometry.pic0SigmaFunctor_isSheaf
  • AlgebraicGeometry.pic0SigmaSheaf

The \(\Sigma \)-extension of the degree-zero Picard functor is a sheaf for the big Zariski topology on schemes.

Proof ▶

The Zariski pretopology is generated by open covers and is stable under base change, so the sheaf condition reduces to elementwise unique amalgamation over an honest open cover \((\iota _i \colon U_i \to Y)\) carrying a compatible family \(x_i = \langle a_i, \xi _i \rangle \) of \(\Sigma \)-elements.

Structure components. Compatibility on pullbacks forces the \(a_i\) to agree on overlaps, so they glue to a unique \(a_Y \colon Y \to \operatorname{Spec}k\) with \(\iota _i \circ a_Y = a_i\) (gluing of scheme morphisms along an open cover).

Fibre components. The cover members induce slice morphisms \((U_i, a_i) \to (Y, a_Y)\) with open-immersion left legs and jointly surjective ranges. The fibres \(\xi _i\) are a compatible family on this slice cover: by the compatibility descent (Lemma 1088(iii)), the \(\Sigma \)-level compatibility of the \(x_i\) descends to slice-level compatibility of the \(\xi _i\). By the morphism-form sheaf property of the degree-zero functor (Theorem 1085) the \(\xi _i\) glue to a unique degree-zero class \(s\) on \((Y, a_Y)\) restricting to each.

Stitching. The \(\Sigma \)-element \(\langle a_Y, s\rangle \) restricts to each \(x_i\) by the amalgamation seam (Lemma 1088(i)). Uniqueness: the structure component of any amalgamation is determined by gluing of morphisms, and its fibre by the separation half of Theorem 1085, again through the seam.

Suppose given a family of schemes \(X_i\) with maps \(f_i \colon \mathrm{yoneda}(X_i) \to \widetilde{\mathrm{pic}^0}(C)\) of big-site sheaves which are relatively representable open immersions, jointly Zariski-locally surjective. Then the local-representability theorem glues the \(X_i\) into a scheme \(J\) representing the \(\Sigma \)-extension, and by \(\Sigma \)-descent (Theorem 1089) the set-valued degree-zero Picard functor is representable on the slice by \(J\) placed over \(\operatorname{Spec}k\) via the structure component of the universal element.

Proof ▶

The local-representability theorem for Zariski sheaves on schemes (mathlib’s 01JJ engine) applies to the sheaf of Theorem 1091 and the given chart family, producing a representation of the \(\Sigma \)-extension by the glued scheme; compose with Theorem 1089.

This remains a valid conditional local-representability theorem. Spelled out, its hypothesis asks for a family of schemes \(X_i\) together with maps \(\mathrm{yoneda}(X_i) \to \widetilde{\mathrm{pic}^0}(C)\) such that

  • each \(f_i\) is relatively representable by an open immersion: for every scheme \(T\) and every \(\Sigma \)-element \(\xi \in \widetilde{\mathrm{pic}^0}(C)(T)\), the fibre product \(\mathrm{yoneda}(X_i) \times _{\widetilde{\mathrm{pic}^0}(C)} T\) is representable by an open subscheme of \(T\) — so each \(f_i\) exhibits \(X_i\) as an open piece of the functor, with the openness verified at every test, not merely at points;

  • the family is jointly Zariski-locally surjective: every element of \(\widetilde{\mathrm{pic}^0}(C)(T)\) is, after restriction to the members of some open cover of \(T\), in the image of some \(f_i\).

These hypotheses are not supplied by the raw admissible Abel map. Its fibres are complete linear systems and can have positive dimension, so that map is neither an open immersion nor an open atlas. Section 8.7 instead restricts the degree-\(g(C)\) Abel map to the locus where \(H^1\) vanishes and the pushforward has rank one. The canonical evaluation divisor identifies that divisor open with the corresponding Picard open. Over a separably closed field, its translates cover every field-valued Picard class and therefore supply the chart family above; finite Galois descent then returns the arbitrary-field representer together with its representation certificate. The larger admissible divisor source remains available for arbitrary-degree divisor geometry, but its positive-dimensional linear systems do not enter this open-atlas construction.

7.78 The Abel element

For a rational point \(P\) of the curve, the class of the diagonal minus the constant graph is a degree-zero family on the test \(T = C\) — the element whose image under the universal correspondence of the representation is the Abel map.

kleiman-picard, abelian-varieties:page-0107 Let \(P \colon \mathbf{1} \to C\) be a rational point of the curve (a morphism from the unit test). The Abel Čech class on the test \(T = C\) is

\[ \mathcal A_P \; :=\; \mathcal{O}_{C \otimes C}(\Delta ) \cdot \mathcal{O}_{C \otimes C}(P \times C)^{-1} \; \in \; \operatorname{Pic}(C \otimes C), \]

the graph class of the identity \(\operatorname{id}_C\) (the diagonal) times the inverse graph class of the constant point \(C \to \mathbf1 \xrightarrow {P} C\) — both factors through the graph divisor of Definition 151, so one degree certificate serves both. The Abel class \(\alpha _P \in \mathrm{picEt}(C, C)\) is the unit image of its relative class. Milne’s cited section assumes \(g(C){\gt}0\); this graph-class construction uses only the rational point \(P\) and therefore also applies in genus zero.

Theorem 1095 The functor-point formula, Čech level

For any test \(T\) and any point \(f \colon T \to C\), the pullback of the Abel Čech class along \(C \lhd f\) is the graph-minus-constant-graph class of \(f\):

\[ (C \lhd f)^{*} \mathcal A_P = \mathcal{O}_{C \otimes T}(\Gamma _f)\cdot \mathcal{O}_{C \otimes T}(\Gamma _{P_T})^{-1}, \]

where \(P_T \colon T \to \mathbf1 \xrightarrow {P} C\) is the constant point of \(T\).

Proof ▶

Base change of the graph class (Theorem 152) sends \(\mathcal{O}_{}(\Gamma _{\operatorname{id}_C})\) to \(\mathcal{O}_{}(\Gamma _{f \circ \operatorname{id}}) = \mathcal{O}_{}(\Gamma _f)\) and \(\mathcal{O}_{}(\Gamma _{P_C})\) to \(\mathcal{O}_{}(\Gamma _{f \circ P_C})\); and \(f \circ P_C = P_T\) by terminality of the unit test (both factor through \(\mathbf1\)). Pullback is a homomorphism, so the product formula follows.

At every field point \(t \colon \operatorname{Spec}K \to C\), the Abel class has degree zero: \(\deg _t(\alpha _P) = 0\). The certificate is a proved equality at every point — no choice is involved.

Proof ▶

By the unit seam (Theorem 1093) the degree is \(\mathrm{relPicDeg}_K\) of the restriction of the relative Abel class along \(t\), which the relative degree reads as \(\deg _{\operatorname{Pic}}\) of the fibre Čech class (Definition 619 on the projected representative, Definition 684). By the functor-point formula (Theorem 1095) at \(f := t\), the fibre class is \(\mathcal{O}_{}(\Gamma _t) \cdot \mathcal{O}_{}(\Gamma _{P_{\operatorname{Spec}K}})^{-1}\) — the ratio of two graph classes of \(K\)-points. Each has degree one by the degree-one certificate (Theorem 682), so the degree is \(1 - 1 = 0\).
